The Unix Bargain

Small tools, sharp edges, fifty years

Composability bought with discoverability. Fifty years on, still the best trade in software.

2 min read3 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 21 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersHow it happenedWho did the workWhere it is contestedCorrectedWhat I changed my mind aboutGo to the sourceReads across to

Two people built it on a spare minicomputer after their employer cancelled the ambitious version. That constraint is the entire design.

If you keep one line

Composability is bought with discoverability — know which side of the trade you're standing on.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Multics was the grand plan: a computing utility, everything for everyone, designed by committee across three organisations. Bell Labs pulled out. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie then built something small on a discarded PDP-7, and in 1973 rewrote it in C. Portability was not the reason. "At the time we did not put much weight on portability," Ritchie wrote later; "interest in this arose later." It turned out to be the load-bearing decision anyway. An operating system you could carry to new hardware was one that could outlive its hardware, which is why code written in the seventies still runs and the machine it was written for is in a museum.

The bargain is explicit: programs do one thing, they speak plain text, and you compose them with pipes. You trade discoverability and safety for composability and leverage. It is a terrible interface for a novice and an extraordinary one for someone who has paid the learning cost. That cost is real, not a personality defect, which is why every generation sincerely tries to replace it and mostly ends up shipping a nicer shell on top.

Plain text as the universal interface is the underrated half. It is lossy, unstructured, and constantly re-parsed, and it is also the reason a tool written in 1975 can be piped into a tool written last week by someone who has never heard of it. Every attempt to replace it with a richer typed protocol has bought correctness and paid in composability, which is the same trade running the other way.

The cultural legacy is stranger than the technical one. Richard Gabriel's 'worse is better' — the argument that the simpler, uglier, shippable design beats the correct and complete one — started as an observation about Unix and Lisp and became a general theory of how technology spreads. Gabriel then spent years arguing against himself in print, which is the most Unix thing about it.

01By the numbers

1969First Unix, in PDP-7 assembly at Bell Labs: Wikipedia, 'Unix'
1973Unix kernel rewritten in C: Dennis Ritchie, 'The Development of the C Language' (1993)
1978McIlroy states the Unix philosophy: do one thing well

02How it happened

  1. 1969Thompson writes the first Unix on a cast-off PDP-7 while his family is away for a month.
  2. 1973Thompson and Ritchie rewrite the kernel in C. Nobody is thinking about portability yet; the 1977 port to the Interdata 8/32 makes it the point.
  3. 1978Doug McIlroy states the philosophy: write programs that do one thing well and work together.
  4. 1983Thompson and Ritchie receive the Turing Award.
  5. 1991Linux begins as a student project and eventually inherits the entire bargain.

03Who did the work

Ken ThompsonWrote the first version in the month his wife and son were away, a week each for the kernel, shell, editor and assembler. Also wrote the paper on trusting trust that should still frighten you.
Dennis RitchieCreated C. Approximately everything you use is written in it or in a descendant of it.
Doug McIlroyInvented the pipe and then wrote down the philosophy it implied, in that order.

04Where it is contested

'Worse is better' is quoted as a rule; Gabriel himself argued both sides for years and never settled it. And the claim that Unix's design is why it won competes with a duller explanation, which Peter Salus documents: the 1956 consent decree kept AT&T out of the software business, so it licensed Unix to universities almost for free and with no support, and a generation learned it, and learned to fix it for each other, because it was there.

05Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 7 · Sept 2026 · Unix and C.

The Unix Bargain dated the rewrite of Unix in C to 1972 and called C a language invented so the system could move. Ritchie's own account puts the kernel rewrite in the summer of 1973 and says portability carried little weight at the time; it became the point with the 1977 port to the Interdata 8/32. The entry also said Thompson wrote the first version in three weeks. By his own account it took the month his wife and son were away.

06What I changed my mind about

I used to think the philosophy caused the success. The licensing accident probably did more. That doesn't make the philosophy wrong — it makes it the thing that let a free system stay useful for fifty years rather than the thing that spread it in the first place.
